On the Orders of the Day:

On
June 8th a question was put to the government by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) with regard to the adulteration of Canadian grain in American ports. I understand from the answer given by the minister on that occasion that an inquiry, or at least a kind of semi-inquiry, was held. The people of western Canada are deeply interested in this matter and I should like to know from the government whether they intend to submit to the House further information in connection with it; and, if not, where such information may be obtained. In other words, is it likely that a report of that inquiry will be published in the immediate future?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
The government have nothing
to add to the reply made a few days ago, for the reason that there was only a verbal report from the officers of the department. After the return of the grain commissioners and the inspector from visits to the ports of New York, Baltimore and Philadelphia, they came to Ottawa and made a verbal report of conditions as they had found them. We now have overseas the Chairman of the Board of Grain Commissioners, and the Chief Grain Inspector at Winnipeg. We hope they will return early next month. They will advise the government as to the condition of grain as they find it on its arrival in England shipped from Canadian as well as United States ports. I have only to add that if Canadian shippers persist in putting grain through by way of the United States they run the risk because the Canadian government has no control over grain once it leaves our own boundaries. My hon. friend, I think, will understand that. Let me say to him and to the House what I said to the members of the London Corn Exchange,- that the grain goes through the United States in bond for the protection of the American people, to make certain that it is not sold. If we sold our grain to Liverpool and subsequently Liverpool sold it to France and France came back with a complaint against the inspection of that grain, surely my hon. friend will understand that we cannot follow it so far, once it has gone into another elevator and broken bulk.

The people are anxious to
know the extent to which there has been adulteration.

Inquiry for Returns-C.N.R.

There has been adulteration
to a very limited extent; it was limited to one port. I may say that we had no real complaint against the port of New York.

Is it the
practice of the minister's department, or of the government generally, to accept verbal reports as a result of inquiries held in the various departments? It seems an extraordinary procedure.
These gentlemen were officers of the department, and every day such officers come into the ministers' offices and advise them of conditions prevailing in their particular branches.

But this
was a special inquiry.

No, it was conducted by
officers of the department.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I had occasion some two weeks ago to refer to failures to bring down orders of the House included among which was one that was passed on the 12th February -I am sure I have the right date-for the production of correspondence which, in the order as passed, was divided into three different catalogues: A, between the members of the government and officials of the Canadian National Railways; B, between members of parliament and the Canadian National Railways, and between certain dates set out in the order; and C, correspondence specially referring to the removal of the late directors and general manager. The government some time ago commenced to bring down this return by instalments, beginning with the portion referring to "correspondence between members of the government and officials." I think it is quite clear the order meant between members of the government and officers of the government and the company. But in filling the order the government has included all manner of trifling correspondence between one agent here and another agent there until a pile of lumber about a foot thick has been brought down. I use the phrase "pile of lumber" advisedly; I do not think the government could have imagined that any such correspondence was called for by the order. I think what should have been brought down is the correspondence between members of the government and leading officials of the
(Mr. Meitjhen.]
company itself. Indeed, the order did not say between any minor officials or officers of the various companies. Consequently, I wish to say that obviously this was not called for, and I think it is only brought down as a method of delaying what the order really calls for. The B and C catalogues have not been started, although we are now four months and more from the passing of the order. These could have been brought down at once, for they cover correspondence between the government and the company relating to the resignation- removal, really-of the directors, which evidently could not be very lengthy but is of importance. I do not think there is any excuse for four months' delay in bringing that correspondence down, but if there is any excuse the worst possible one is the searching out of correspondence between a station agent and some other minor agent of another company relating to a culvert, as if any such thing was called for by the terms of the order itself. I must ask that the substance of the order, and particularly the two B and C catalogues which could easily be complied with, be complied with now, and that the waste of money along the line at present being pursued be stopped.
Secondly, on May 14th an order was passed for a return showing orders for rolling stock and equipment given since October 4, 1922. This order has not been complied with, and certainly only a comparatively brief return would be necessary. I know of no reason for the delay. There are other orders as well, but I am emphasizing these two at the moment.

On motion of Hon. Ernest Lapointe, (Minister of Marine and Fisheries), the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure to make provision for the improvement and management of the harbour of Three Rivers, in the province of Quebec, and to provide:
1.	That the commissioners appointed under this Act shall be incorporaited under the name of the "Three Rivers Hartxmr Commissioners".
2.	That boundaries of the harbour be defined; harbour commissioners and a harbour master, a deputy harbour master and other officers be appointed; and rules and regulations, and a tariff of rates and dues be made.
3.	That the jurisdiction of the commissioners be defined, as well as their powers as to expropriation of lands and the making of by-laws, the collection of rents, and the borrowing of money.
4.	That the commissioners shall expend the moneys collected, after payment of the salary of the harbour master and the necessary expenses of maintenance of the harbour, in improving the harbour and its appurtenances according to plans to be approved by the minister.
5.	That regulations as to seizures, penalties, the application of the same and the general administration of the harbour be established.
Will the minister tell us how much the port of Three Rivers has improved as to importance, sailings, and so on? Perhaps he can give us the history of the port; it ought to be very interesting.

There has been a misconception on the part of some hon. members that by this proposed legislation it was sought to create a new commission. The harbour commission of Three Rivers was created by statute as far back as 1882. Some of the provisions of that statute are inadequate, and the main changes now proposed are these: The harbour commissions were formerly composed of manjr members- representatives of the board of trade, of the city council, and so on. It has been thought that that arrangement is too cumbersome. So the Three Rivers Commission will henceforth be composed of three members as in the case of the other important harbour commissions. The boundaries of the harbour are better defined than they were before. We have followed almost word for word the provisions of the enactment-the latest of its kind-creating a commission for the harbour of Vancouver.
The only change, Ihen, is a better definition of the boundaries and a reduction of the number of commissioners from an unmentioned number to three?
Five to three.
Is there any other change?
There are many other changes. I have said that we have followed the same lines as in the case of the bill for Vancouver.

Is the Three Rivers commission the same, generally speaking, as the other commissions? For example, has the harbour been taken over by the Dominion authority, or are the commissioners local commissioners? Is it the municipality
Three Rivers Harbour

or the Dominion that is financing the harbour?

The harbour commission of Three Rivers was created by statute in 1882. At that time we had no docks except those of Canada Steamship Lines. Permission was obtained to borrow $82,000, which was advanced by the Minister of Finance. The harbour commission consisted of three men appointed by the government, together with the mayor of the city and the president of the board of trade. In 1892 an amendment to the act creating the harbour commission was adopted; owing to the increase of trade and the general expansion which had taken place, permission was given to the harbour commission to borrow $190,000 for the building of docks. A cement dock was built by the Dominion government and turned over to the commission for administration. The commission administer the whole of the harbour. They make all charges for harbour dues, wharfage, dockage, and so on; they draw up the schedule for fees or tolls to be paid. Exerything they do has to be submitted to the Governor in Council for approval. Their powers are practically those of the other harbour commissions. But, so as to bring about uniformity, I have asked, in accordance with requests made to me, that the lines followed be the same as those laid down in the case of the other large commissions, particularly the Vancouver commission, which is the latest and most modem. There is a change in the limits of the harbour of Three Rivers. The old limits were, west, a prolongation of the divisional line between the parish and the city of Three Rivers across the river, including the south shore, and east a prolongation of a line-
My hon. friend need not give the details.

We have taken the natural boundary lines, making an increase east as well as an increase west. To the north it is the same, being co-extensive with the limits of the city of Three Rivers. The change of the harbour limits is necessary owing to the cropping up of new industries along the water front of the St. Lawrence and the St. Maurice rivers. The object is to enable the exercise of some control as to how these things shall be done, and also to provide for the collection of harbour dues for the raising of a revenue to maintain the docks, and so on. The interest due on the debentures of the harbour commission is regularly paid; there is also a sinking fund into which amounts have regularfSir Henry Drayton.]
ly been placed, except for a period during the war. Everything has been conducted legally and in due form; it is just to modernize the harbour that we are asking for this legislation.
I am sure the House will be glad to assist the hon. member in modernizing Three Rivers if possible.
It is the harbour we want to modernize.

About when were the
present commissioners appointed?

I do not remember the
exact date-since we have come into power. I recommended that the three commissioners appointed by the former government be replaced by the three who now hold office.
I suppose that was the process of modernizing?
Yes, that was the beginning of the modernizing.

I hope it will not be the beginning of failure to pay interest or to conduct the board on a proper business basis. My hon. friend says that everything had been properly done; the interest has been paid, and so on,. I do not know whether that was the reason for the replacing of the former commissioners. What is to be done in the way of improvements?

There is no programme yet. A coal dock which was built by the Department of Public Works has not been turned over to the commission-it is still under the department-but as the other docks were built they were turned over by the department to the harbour commission. As I say, no definite scheme of improvement has yet been adopted, but I hope something in that line will be done before long.
What salaries are paid the commissioners?
They are not paid any salaries at all.
They get no remuneration?
No remuneration.
That is why nobody complained about being dismissed.

I would like to ask whether paragraph 4 of the resolution intends a change or not. Under it the commissioners are to expend the moneys collected, after payment of the salary of the harbour master and the neces-

Three Rivers Harbour
sary expenses of maintenance of the harbour, improving the harbour and its appurtenances according to plans to be approved by the minister. There is no provision there for the payment of interest or sinking fund. Will that be in the bill?
Yes.

It is in the bill.

On section 3-Interpretation.

I would ask my hon. friend whether this interpretation clause is the standard clause, to be found, for example, in such a bill as the one respecting the Vancouver Harbour Board. Are there any changes made here beyond changes of names?
I think it is the same absolutely.
If my hon. friend can tell me that is the fact I am quite content to take his word.
It is the same thing.

Section stands.

On section 5-Commissioner.
There is a change made here apparently. My hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) told us I think that the commissioners were not paid any salary.
No.
But under this bill it is now proposed to pay them a salary.
Yes, under the control of the Governor in Council.

There is an express clause here to the effect that for their services the president and the other commissioners may be paid out of the revenues of the harbour such remuneration as the Governor in Council may determine. I rather understood from my hon. friend that there was to be no change in that regard. Apparently there is to be a change.

If my hon. friend understood that, I never intended to give such an impression. The harbour of Three Rivers is increasing in importance every day, and the development of the port requires, like the ports of Montreal and Quebec, men who will give their whole time to the work. It would not be fair to ask them to give their full time to this work without remuneration. I would point out that this bill has no retroactive effect, and this provision is made in anticipation of the development of the harbour at Three Rivers and of the St. Maurice region, which is developing very fast. We have not got the accommodation we ought to have now to take care of the traffic. This clause is to provide that when conditions justify it the commissioners shall be paid a salary which will be determined by the Governor in Council.
Of course the bill is not made retroactive. If it was, perhaps somebody would say that it was being done to help the commissioners whose heads are being cut off.
Leave it to me not to help them.
What is happening under this bill is this. The commissioners who have carried on the work properly and made a first-rate financial showing-
Do not insist too much upon that.
I am only taking what my hon. friend from Three Rivers said a few moments ago. He said-

They were paying the
interests and sinking fund except for a period during the war.

I thought everything had gone on all right afterwards. That is doing pretty well to keep things paid up and not to be a charge on the government at all. While that was done under these commissioners who served without salary-

It is being done now.
Three Rivers Harbour
Apparently one of the real motives behind this bill is that the three friends whom my hon. friend has put in to modernize the commission are to be paid.

The three men who are
there now do not want the money first. They are all men of great ability. I can tell my hon. friend what their business is. One of them is the managing director of the St. Maurice Lumber Company, which is a subsidiary of the international company which has mills in New Brunswick and in Nova Scotia too, if I am not mistaken. They have a paper mill in Three Rivers, which some of my friends in the House had occasion to visit a short time ago when they were in Three Rivers. It is the largest paper mill, I think, on this side of the line. Another of the gentlemen is a hardware merchant who has made a success of his business; and the other is a wholesale drygoods man. Every one of them can live without a salary as commissioner, but if we are going to pass an act to incorporate a commission we must look ahead to the future development of the port, and I am satisfied, in view of the development of the St. Maurice region, that before many years the harbour of Three Rivers will require a staff of engineers and men who will have to devote their whole time to the interests of the harbour. We have power galore, and more is being developed; we have also a fine water front. There is no reason at all why the port should not develop and take care of all the manufactured products which are made in that district as far up as La Tuque. I would not ask parliament to pass a bill to pay some friends of mine. My hon. friend may rest assured I shall never do that.

I have no doubt from what my hon. friend says that thes-e commissioners can get along very well without the salary. I have no doubt, further, in view of what he says, that it is not a question of salary first with them at all, nor do I think in view again of what he says, that it is a question of money coming afterwards.
Afterwards?
Afterwards, yes.
In the future.
So far as these gentlemen are concerned I am quite sure they do not want any salary.
Oh, no.

I do not know why my hon. friend is insisting on it.
I Mr. Bureau. 1
For the future.

Unless it is that, while we now have three first rate commissioners, as my hon. friend tells us, in the near future these gentlemen are to give up their jobs and somebody is to be appointed who wants the salary.
Oh, no.

That is what
my hon. friend says.

To the pure all things
are pure.

This is exactly the
same provision as in the statutes concerning the Vancouver Harbour Commission, the Quebec Harbour Commission, and the Montreal Harbour Commission. Why should we strike out this clause because it refers to Three Rivers?

The only reason I was referring to it at all is that, while we were told that no salaries whatever were to be paid to the commissioners, yet it will be possible in this case to render these offices, offices of emolument.

There was no salary formerly, and I do not know whether there will ever be one; it all depends upon the development of the harbour. Why should we make an exception in the case of Three Rivers and strike out that clause in this bill which is in the other statutes?
The minister says there are salaries in the case of certain other harbour commissioners.
In the case of Montreal, Quebec and Vancouver there are.

What about Hamilton
and Toronto?
There is no salary.

No provision for it? It would have been well for the minister to have said that in this case so that the House would know the facts. The truth is that in case of large harbours where the commissioners have to give all their time the House has provided that salaries may be paid; in the case of the smaller harbours it has not. There is no desire on the part of a single individual in this House to discriminate against Three Rivers; but I was a little doubtful whether the government were going to the trouble of introducing a bill to reduce the number of commissioners and for no other purpose. I wondered when the truth was going to come out.

Three Rivers Harbour

We want to enlarge the
limits of the harbour.

If salaries are paid I
do not think there will be any further bill to reduce the number of harbour commissioners.
You think we will increase them?
If the harbour is on a par with Vancouver and Montreal, and- what is the other one?
Quebec.

Those are the three
that are on a par. There is no objection to these appointments provided they are not made as they were in Hamilton. I certainly would not urge that. I would like to have the opinion of some members of the government as to the value to the country of the changes that were made in Hamilton, for example. I hope there will be no provision to introduce salaries in the Hamilton case. I understand, they took the recommendation of the president of the Liberal Association and because the recommendation was so outrageous, one or two of the men appointed being in his employ, there was such an explosion in the Liberal Association that the president was removed from office. This was all due to the awful character of the recommendation which, of course, coming from the president of the association, the government accepted. That is what was done in Hamilton. I hope the minister will not carry that precedent any further, and, that in cases where he has submitted to patronage exploitation so fully as in the Hamilton case he will not go on and pay salaries there too.

That is an interesting
bit of history that I was not acquainted with at all.
The minister was overseas when the explosion occurred.

The ex-Minister of Finance did not represent correctly what I said. Talking about the commission as organized under the statutes of 1882, he asked me if the commissioners were paid, and I said, "No." That was the five commissioners. I did not say that they would not be paid hereafter, but I made the statement that this clause was copied from the Vancouver bill. I know there is' a future for the harbour of Three Rivers. This is a tidewater port, not an inland port, and there are always two or three ocean vessels there. My hon. friends who visited Three Rivers a short time ago will remember that there were a couple of ocean
ships at the dock on that occasion, but with present conditions it is not necessary that the commissioners should devote their whole time to the work. As I said, I hope parliament will, before long, acknowledge the necessity of increasing the facilities in the harbour of Three Rivers on account of the development of the back country. The region of the St. Lawrence alone now produces 1,500 tons a day of pulp and paper, and other paper mills and other industries are going up. I think that part of the country-of course some of my hon. friends may smile at the prediction-will, within a quarter of a century, be the industrial centre of Canada.
Yes, we smile.

I want my prediction to go on Hansard. Nature has provided Three Rivers with a splendid harbour. We have a tidewater port, the finest on the St. Lawrence. And I say, with all due consideration for my Montreal and Quebec
4 p.m. friends, we have no tide. I think Three Rivers is the only tidewater port in the world that has no tide.
Oh, oh.

The current never changes, it flows down twelve months in the year. There may be a backing up of six or seven inches in the height of the tide but it always flows the same way. There is depth of water galore, there is power galore, and a splendid field for labour. Some of the younger generation in this House will live to see remarkable developments at Three Rivers. I am afraid the Quebec harbour will be put in the shade as compared with Three Rivers.
Section agreed to.
We might perhaps revert to section 3. I might answer my hon. friend now by saying that the interpretation clause is practically the same as in the Vancouver Act.
Exactly the same except that in the latter case the word "Vancouver" appears?

I would not
think there was any necessity for a marine railway at Three Rivers any more than at Quebec?

The corporation may own and operate by any motive power, all kinds of tracks, appliances, apparatus, plant and machinery for the purpose of increasing the usefulness of the harbour or facilitating traffic therein.
Are the present rails owned by the commissioners, or by the company?

There is an agreement between the commission and the Canadian Pacific Railway. I think the commission leases the ground to the company, or the company leases their tracks, I could not tell which it is, I have not looked at the agreement for a long time; but it is either one or the other. The company are obliged to let anyone that comes use the tracks. I am speaking from memory, but I think the tracks are practically public tracks controlled by the commission.
Has this bill been printed?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.
We have no copies of it.
I have not a copy-except a typewritten copy.
There are eighteen miles of railway in the harbour of Quebec.

I do not think the Harbour Commissioners of Quebec run a marine railway. I think they use rather the company power. My recollection is-you can correct me if I am wrong-that those tracks were put down by the railway company, and not by the commission, and the railway company operates them.
They are owned and operated by the commission.
Not in Three Rivers. In Three Rivers there is an agreement between the railway company and the harbour commissioners.
I object to the bill going through without copies being furnished. What chance have I to say anything about a bill when I do not know anything about it?
If my hon. friend objects, of course I cannot proceed any further.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The objection should have been raised on the motion to go into committee. Objection can be raised to the clauses in committee, but not to the bill being considered in committee.

I am not objecting, but 1 think it puts us at a disadvantage. I am particularly interested in this subject from the standpoint of the city of St. John, which, I hope, some day will put itself in a position to take advantage of the harbour commission legislation. I was anxious to follow this bill for the purpose of seeing how certain problems that would affect St. John might be dealt with. I have not made an objection because I did not wish to hold up the business of the House, but I think it might Le arranged that there should be a proper distribution of bills before we are called upon to consider them. I know that in much smaller establishments than this it is impossible to get a bill which is not printed dealt with, except by specially asking unanimous consent to do so. The rule of this House seems to be different, and this House proceeds unless somebody stops it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The bill is always distributed among members of the House, except when the resolution is put through the House on the same day as the bill is introduced. We have only two or three of these bills printed this afternoon, or rather we have the proof sheets. This resolution was introduced this afternoon and got its second reading, and the House went into committee. That is the reason the bill is not distributed.

I do not think the Chairman's interpretation is quite correct. It is true a bill of this kind can only follow a resolution, and nothing else can go on, except by unanimous consent. But I do not think it is correct to say that the House is competent to go into committee on a bill until the English and French copies have been distributed. I have never seen it done, and I have not seen unanimous consent asked for it. I think it would be a very grave irregularity, and a bad precedent on the part of anybody at any stage, to put through a bill copies of which bon. members have not in their possession.

We yield.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to mention a matter of another character in connection with this act in the hope that if the minister sees fit to adopt my suggestion he may introduce the necessary amendment. It is a matter in which considerable injustice has been done to shipping masters and mates, I believe more or less inadvertently. It has been brought to a head. by a recent ruling of a supreme court judge in the West, and I think his ruling is due to a mistake in the wording of the act.
Section 96 of the Canada Shipping A.ct provides that steamers "going" from one port to another in Canada or on any coasting voyage shall carry certificated masters. But that section does not provide any penalty for nonobservance of this law. The section which does prescribe a penalty is section 120, which provides that any master or mate engaged in such a vessel which goes on any voyage"-that is the way it is worded, "goes on any voyage," and that is what the decision hangs on- shall be subject to a penalty, and so forth.
Some years later it appears to have been thought advisable to change this section, and in 1908 the act was amended by chapter 65. So far as I can understand it, the intention of the amendment was not only to put a penalty and a responsibility upon the master of the vessel who went from one place to another uncertificated, but also to provide a penalty for the owners. I think that was the intention of the amendment to the act, but unfortunately it was worded somewhat differently, and instead of using the words "going from one place to another," the amendment reads "any ship trading" from one point to another or on inland waters, as the case may be.
Canada Shipping Act

A test case was taken before the courts in Vancouver last year, when the Merchant Seamen's Guild prosecuted a man who was taking a boat on the coast without any certificate whatever. But it appeared that the boat contained only goods belonging to the owner of the vessel, and the decision went against the guild. An appeal was taken to the supreme court, but the judge there also decided against the guild on the ground that the boat in question was not "trading" ' within the meaning of the act. It was perfectly clear that they had been engaged in going from one port to another, but they had not been engaged in trading in the opinion of the judge because they were carrying only the goods of the owner. Now, it is easy for this House to see that the danger of a boat being in charge of an uncertificated man is equally great whether the goods on that boat belong to its owner or to somebody else. It is an absurdity to say that it is correct and safe for a man uncertificated to be in charge of a boat if the goods belong to the owner of the boat, but that it is all wrong and dangerous if the goods belong to someone else. I think that only needs to be stated to show its absurdity. There is also the sense of responsibility on the part of the master or mate to be taken into account. A certificated master or mate who takes a chance and runs his boat on the rocks or has a collision loses his certificate and therefore his livelihood; but an uncertificated man has no such scruples, he can afford to take a chance and if he does wreck his boat he can go out and get another if somebody is foolish enough to employ him.
There is no question of cost because I am informed that a considerable number of these certificated men are willing Jo work for the wages given to the uncertificated men. How the former came to be ousted from their positions is that during the war they went on ships engaged in the war and when they came back they found their old positions taken by uncertificated men perhaps unavoidably because no others could be obtained at the time. But those conditions no longer exist and it is perfectly just and proper that these certificated men should now be restored to their former positions both for their own benefit and for the safety of the public.
I may quote one sentence regarding the decision of the judge. It is as follows:
The new section says "trading.'' His Lordship held that parliament must have had some reason for making the ohange, and that the word "trading'' was deliberately substituted for "going".
The learned judge evidently was never in this parliament, or he would have known that we often do things without any particular
[Mr. Neill.j
reason, and that words drawn up by someone somewhat unfamiliar with the circumstances sometimes slip into our legislation. Besides, for some ten years this section has never been called in question. It was taken to mean that trading did cover the conditions I have mentioned. But now that this judge has ruled in the opposite direction, I submit it is desirable to go back to the old rendering of section 120 dealing with the point, so the word "trading" will be altered to mean as in the original act, namely, a boat going from one port to another.
I have the details of the particular case before me, and I shall be glad to furnish them to the minister's officers if they wish to go into it.

My hon. friend is making a case which appears very strong and which favourably impresses me, at any rate. But as I told him some time ago, it is the intention of the department and of the government to revise the whole Shipping Act next session if at all possible. The object of the present amendment is merely to deal with questions of procedure and to harmonize the law in some points with the board of trade regulations in England. No important changes are made. I would ask my hon. friend to leave the matter for the present. Speaking from the first view I have of it, I think there is no reason for making the differentiation that he has pointed out; I think the word "going" would be a better word there than the word "trading." However, I promise him that the matter will engage my consideration.

Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Pictou, Acting Minister of National Defence) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, (1) that is is expedient to amend the provisions of the Militia Pension Act by providing that the period of service entitling officers, retired compulsorily, to pension, shall be twenty years; and that any officer so retired, who served on active service during the Great War and was appointed to the Force on or after the 1st January, 1919, and prior to 31st December, 1921, and since such appointment has served continuously in the Force for not less than ten years, shall be entitled to pension as provided in section four of the said act.
2. That the period of service required of every militiaman to entitle him to pension shall be twenty years, or fifteen years if incapacitated for duty by infirmity of mind or body, and he shall be subject to return to service if he ceases to be incapacitated, and if he has completed fifteen but less than twenty years service, his pension shall be an annual sum equal to one-fiftieth of his annual pay and allowances for every completed year of service.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
The purpose of this resolution is to bring the situation in regard to militia pensions back to where it was previous to the legislation of 1919. Under the original provisions of the Militia Pension Act, which has been in force in this country for a great number of years, an officer could be compulsorily retired at the end of twenty years, and on retirement, if his record was good, he was entitled to receive a certain amount of pension. At the end of twenty-five years he could retire voluntarily and receive a pension. Previous to 1919, so far as the officers were concerned, they contributed every year a certain percentage out of their salary to the pension fund, and the fund was self sustaining. Non-commissioned officers and men made no contribution to the fund but were entitled to receive a pension after twenty years' service with good conduct. In 1919, after the war, an amendment was made which provided for the reduction of the period of service, as regards the officers, from twenty years to ten, and a similar reduction in the time of service was made in the case of the men. The result of the change has been a very large increase in the amount paid in pensions. Thus in the year 1919-20 the amount of pensions paid to officers and men amounted to only $225,000 whereas, as a result of the amendment shortening the period of service, the amount so paid in 1922-23 reached the total of $550,000-pension payments were actually doubled. The object of the amendment of 1919 was to look after quite a number of competent officers who had seen service during the war but who after-
253i
wards came into the department and were attached to the permanent force. Since that time there has been quite a retirement of officers, which accounts for the large increase in the amount of pensions. Altogether 369 officers and warrant officers have been retired since July 7, 1919, and in the case of noncommissioned officers and men the retirements number 295. The result has been that the cost of pensions has increased very materially. There is no further reason why the short period of service should be continued any longer. It is the view of the officers of the department that we should revert to the twenty-year period, to qualify for a pension. As regards those officers who came in between 1919 and last year, who were veterans of the war and enlisted on the faith of the ten years' service, it is provided that the ten-year provision should still apply to them. In all other respects it is proposed to revert to the twenty-year period as regards all the officers and men connected with the department. There have been a large number of withdrawals by non-commissioned officers and men who have served less than twenty years. The applications for withdrawal have become so numerous that it was felt it would not be wise to continue the pension at great cost to the country for mere service in the ranks for a period of ten years without any contribution to the fund on the part of the men.

The hon. member for

If the change suggested by my hon. friend were a desirable one it would probably apply properly to all insurance policies. I do not say that he -S a consenting party to this section of the bill, but I do not think he would object if he were here, the Superintendent of Insurance having explained the matter to him.

I would call the minister's attention to a provision that seems to be usual in modern insurance acts and which I do not think has been included in this bill, although I may observe that I ran over the bill hastily, my attention having been called to it only to-day. I have looked up the Insurance Act of New Brunswick and I know that it is the same in effect, and I think the wording is also the same, as in many of the western provinces. As I read this bill, while I think it is intended to a certain extent to help the insured, yet there are some difficulties that may arise. At least there are some forms of protection given by the ordinary fire insurance acts that do not seem to be extended to the insured in this case. Let me quote from the New Brunswick statute:
In any one of the following cases:
(a)	Where, by reason of necessity, accident or mistake, the conditions of any contract of fire insurance on property in this province as to the proof to be given to the insurer after the occurrence of a fire, have not been strictly complied with; or
(b)	Where, after a statement	or	proof of loss	hasbeen given in good faith by	or	on behalf	of	theassured in pursuance of any proviso or condition of such contract, the insurer, through its agent or otherwise, objects to the loss upon other grounds than for imperfect compliance with such conditions or does not, within a reasonable time after receiving such statement or proof, notify the assured in writing that such statement or proof is objected	to,	and what	are	theparticulars in which the same	is	alleged to	be	defective, and so from time to time; or
And this is the important one:
(c)	Where, for any other reason, the court or judge before whom a question relating to such insurance is tried or inquired into, considers it inequitable that the insurance should be deemed void or forfeited by reason of imperfect compliance with such conditions, no objection to the sufficiency of such statement or proof or amended or supplemental statements or proof (as the case may be) shall, in any such cases, be allowed as a discharge of the liability of the company on such contract of insurance wherever entered into.
It is a little difficult to follow these sections as one reads them, but the provisions they contain have been given effect to, and amplified if anything in the interpretation of them by the Supreme Court of Canada. I do not want to delay the bill, but I should like the Superintendent of Insurance to consider the sections I have read, which pro-
Insurance Act

bahly have not been called to his attention, lie might give some thought to the expediency of including them in this bill and so putting the insurance of automobiles on a parity with insurance in other cases.

On section 2-Advances during construction on first class docks.

Will the minister explain
what the changes are?

The amendment
deals with those sections which have to do with the payment of progress subsidy during the construction. Previous to 1917 subsidies were not paid until the dock was completed. In 1917 there was an amendment to the act which provided that in the case of first class docks, whether floating or graving docks, process subsidy might be paid during the construction, and provision was made that when it had been established to the satisfaction of the minister that not less than $1,000,000 had been spent on the work and the material used in the construction of the dock, a subsidy of 41 per cent might be paid cm 75 per cent of the cost of the work done and material provided at the time of such payment. In 1919 an amendment to the act made similar provision in the case of second class dry docks and floating docks when mot less than $500,000 had been expended. This left a percentage of 25 per cent of the cost of the work done and materials provided, as a drawback or increasing guarantee as the work proceeded to its ultimate completion.
The present amendment provides that when either a graving or floating dock of the first or second class is three-quarters or 75 per cent, completed, subsidy at the rate of 4| per cent may be paid on 90 per cent of the cost of work done and materials provided, thus decreasing the 25 per cent drawback to ten per cent, which is ample for a work which is three-quarters done. In ordinary contract? ten per cent is ail that is requested as security in the first place, and in the case of larger works running into million? of dohars, five per cent is all that it has been the practice to ask. Then as the work proceeded undpr these contracts, it has been the practice tc, return portions of the security and drawback.
To give a simple illustration of how this works out, assume the cost :>f the dock to be
Dry Dock Subsidies Act

$1,000. When the dock is three-quarters completed, or $750 has been spent, the largest progress subsidy the contractors could get would be 4J per cent on three-quarters of $750. That leaves $187.50 worth of work on which no subsidy is allowed as the department's guarantee. It is considered that after the three-quarters completion stage has been reached, 25 per cent is too large a drawback to retain and it is proposed to pay a subsidy on 90 per cent of the work done. To illustrate : When $900 worth of work has been done under the amendment now proposed, subsidy may be paid on $810, which still leaves $90 value of work done as a guarantee for the performance of the remaining $100 worth of work to complete the dock, when the entire subsidy would be payable.
I think the amendment is a fair one. It does not increase the subsidy or the liability at all, but merely increases the amount of subsidy that may be paid as the dock nears completion, increasing the amount from 75 to 90 per cent of the work done.

I just want to draw the attention of the minister to a case that was brought to light in this House last year, that of the construction of two ships at Prince Rupert. Payments had been made as the work on these boats progressed, and then when the contractors failed to complete their contract it was found that it cost a good deal more than the difference between what they had been paid and the amount of their contract for the government to have the ships completed. I do not think the minister has given us a very good reason for making this change. The amount which he is going to retain under this amendment seems to me very small, and I would like the minister to state whether some concrete case has come before his department which has led him tc think this change is necessary or advisable, having in mind the conditions which were brought to light last year in regard to the construction of these ships at Prince Rupert. In that case, if I remember rightly, the department had a bond to cover default on the part of the contracting parties, but the department never collected that amount from the bond company. Would the minister tell us whether some concrete case has come before his department which has made him think it is necessary or wise to make this change?	.

I might point out that the amendment proposed would apply to only the two dry docks which are now being built, one at St. John, New Brunswick, and the other at Vancouver. The St. John dry 	! J 3X1
dock has reached a stage of over three-fourths completion, and there was a request from the promoters of that work that this amendment should be made. We have canvassed the situation very carefully. The cost of the dock for subsidy purposes was $5,500,000. In December of 1922 the engineers certified that $4,049,980 worth ot work had been done, leaving a balance at that time of $1,450,000 to complete. Since that I am advised that $750,000 worth of work has been done, leaving only a balance of $700,000 to complete the dock. The total bond issue authorized under the subsidy agreement on completion of the dock is $3,826,272. Ponds have been issued to date to the amount of $2,113,422 leaving a balance of $1,712,000.
My hon. friend will appreciate that this work now is very considerably over three-fourths completed. As far as the department is concerned we have canvassed the situation very carefully and we feel satisfied that by retaining ten per cent and allowing them to issue up to ninety per cent the department will be fully protected. The case at Prince Rupert to which my hon. friend refers is not in line with the building that is going on at St. John. In the case to which he refers these were force account contracts, as I understand it, and there was great difficulty and eventually failure to complete. The work at St. John, on the other hand, is going on satisfactorily and it is felt that there will be no danger in allowing them to issue bonds up to 90 per cent.

Just one word more. I expect that in the case of the construction of the ships at Prince Rupert to which I referred the Department of Marine and Fisheries thought they were quite safe in advancing the percentage that they did, but on account of poor service, poor inspection, it seems to me in that department, there was a considerable loss sustained by the treasury of this country. I cannot but feel that the minister in this case is making a mistake in changing the regulations to the extent he proposes here.

If the cases were the same, if the principle of the subsidy was the same as in the case of these unfortunate boats that were being built, the hon. member would be absolutely right, but it is not the same. We are not putting up money here at all. All we do is to put up 4^ per cent of the money that has been put into the undertaking; in other words, we are not risking capital one way or the other in this subsidy. In the other case my hon. friend is quite right.

House again in committee on Bill No. 85 to amend the Naturalization Acts, 1914 and 1920, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The committee has under consideration section 4.
On section 4-Repeal.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. COPP (Secretary of State):
speechtext:
When the bill was before the committee a week or two ago there was some objection to section 4 with regard to changes in connection with the administration of the act. Section 4, as originally submitted to the committee, had
for its purpose a change in the method of making application for naturalization before judges. It proposed, instead, to have such application made direct to the Secretary of State. There was considerable opposition with respect to this point at that time. I have given the matter careful consideration in the hope of being able to devise some other system which would expedite the administration of the act, and at the same time surround it with every possible safeguard. I have not been able to do so, and to save the time of the House I have decided to withdraw those sections of the bill regarding administration and leave the act as it stood originally. I therefore desire, Mr. Chairman, to amend section 4 by striking out all the words before the word "and" in the twenty-first line and deleting the word "are" in the'twenty-second line and inserting between the figures 1920 and the word "repealed" the following' "10 and 11 George V, Chap. 59 is hereby." Section 4 will then be in this form:
Section 7 of the Naturalization Act 1920, 10 and 11 George V, chapter 59 is hereby repealed.
That refers entirely to the amendment passed in 1920 requiring ten years' residence prior to naturalization. The change I am now suggesting simply makes the law as it was up to 1920, which required only five years' residence for naturalization.

I rather regret that the minister has seen fit to amend this section. I find it very hard to blame him, because there certainly was opposition from every section of the House, and I think it arose first from his own benches, the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) challenging the section on the ground that it would take away business from the lawyers and encourage more red tape in the department. I believe, however, that many hon. members opposed the section not knowing just how it affected us in some of the newer districts in the West, and possibly in northern Ontario as well. In these new districts the settlers, who are largely foreign-speaking people, find it a very considerable hardship to go before a judge at some place involving a four or five days' absence from home, to say nothing of the travelling expenses incidental thereto and lawyers' fees, because, although it is not absolutely necessary for them to engage a lawyer, they do not understand our institutions very well and very few of them care to appear in court and speak on their own behalf. I am inclined to think that a good deal of the opposition to this section came from men of the legal fraternity because it
Naturalization Acts

meant a loss of business, and I was very sorry to see that attitude on their part.
I have in mind the case of a man in my own constituency, a very fine type of citizen, who appeared before the judge in April last at considerable expense, for he had to be away from home about five days. For some reason or other the judge deferred action at that time. In October last the man was notified to appear again, but this was impossible as he was just in the middle of his threshing, and his non-appearance meant the cancellation of his application. Now, he has to begin all over again and incur further travelling expenses and court fees. That man thinks an injustice has been done him. When I saw him last he pointed out to me that some of his neighbours had settled down quite peaceably and contentedly and were not particularly anxious whether they took on the responsibilities of citizenship or not. He reminded me what this meant in case of another war- that his neighbours would not be citizens, even though they had been in the country twenty years, and their boys might not be conscripted, while his would be. He was prepared to accept the responsibilities of citizenship, but the government of the country apparently put various stumbling blocks in his way.
After all, a judge's examination in these cases does not amount to a great deal. He asks a few questions of the applicant, but he has no opportunity of knowing whether the man is a desirable citizen or not; whereas under the other system the examination was left largely to the mounted police, and I think they undoubtedly did get a good deal of valuable information. I think a valuable service could be done both to the country and to applicants for naturalization by leaving the examination to the mounted police, and I hope at some future time the minister will see fit to introduce an amendment to this end.
As I understand the minister, the amendment is simply a restoration of the qualifications as they were before the change, with the adoption of the provisions of the Imperial Act?
Five years' residence.

I congratulate the minister upon the decision he has come to. I thought, and still think, that something might be done between now and another session to get rid of the difficulty which has been spoken of by my hon. friend (Mr. Campbell) and yet not give us the mounted police in the Maritime fMr. Campbell.]
provinces and the other settled parts of the Dominion. I believe this can be done in a better way than was originally proposed under this bill.

In the light
of the conditions that have been explained to him by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) does the minister propose to take any steps to make it easier for those who desire to obtain citizenship by arranging for the judge to meet them in centres more convenient than the judicial centre of the district?

I realize as fully as anyone in this House that it does seem inadvisable to leave it to one individual to say whether an applicant may become naturalized or not, and in the amendments I introduced I was only trying to g6t an easy method, surrounded with all the safeguards possible, to enable men to become naturalized. As I have withdrawn the sections regarding administration,
I propose to have my department take up the question with the various judges to see if we cannot get more hearty co-operation in dealing with applications for naturalization. I hope as a result we will have a little more ' activity and assistance in this regard. We hope during the recess to be able to work out some scheme to facilitate naturalization, surrounded at all times, of course, by all the necessary safeguards.

As I understand the minister, we now revert to the old law. I certainly think that a judge is in the best position to decide whether or not an applicant is fit for naturalization and should have power to issue the certificate. I am not in favour of the former amendments by virtue of which the judge only has power to make an investigation. I really think that naturalization should be completely in the hands of the judge or of the Secretary of State. As a practising lawyer, I do not think that naturalization can be regarded as a judicial proceeding, and where the application is not contested I am of opinion that a lawyer would not be entitled to charge any fee for the preparation of the papers. In my view the bill as it was first presented, providing that application should be made directly to the Secretary of State, was certainly preferable to the former procedure, and I am sorry the minister has seen fit to withdraw those sections.
I hope after he has had an opportunity to study the matter further he will during next session introduce another bill embodying the provisions which are now withdrawn.

I am glad to hear the minister say that he proposes to take this matter up with the judges. I would ask him not to overlook the great convenience which would accrue to applicants for naturalization if he could arrange for special sittings to be held at various places easy of access. This has been done in the past by some judges, but others have not been willing to go among these people. Frequently one will find a community of thirty or forty people living at quite a distance from the centre of the judicial district, and if it could be arranged for a judge to hold special sittings, and to simplify the process as much as possible without sacrificing any of the necessary safeguards, and so enable these people to dispense with legal assistance,-which it seems to me is unnecessary in most cases-they would be encouraged to apply for naturalization, and the responsibilities of citizenship would have a good effect in the community.

Concerning expenses, in
the province of Quebec, at all events, an applicant for naturalization must pay fees to the clerk of the court for lodging his petition , and copies of his application. Although these fees are not very heavy, I do not think the applicant for naturalization should have to incur them.

In answer to my hon. friend
(Mr. Millar), I realize that the greatest difficulties surrounding the administration of the Naturalization Act occur in the western provinces, and as I do not know where the judges hold their regular sittings, if hon. members from the West will be good enough to communicate with me and suggest where special sittings should be held at intervals, I shall be glad to convey the information to the judges of the various districts and see if such sittings can be arranged.

With regard to the status of those who have applied in the past for naturalization but were refused because they were of alien enemy birth, I have in mind a particular case of a gentleman whose father emigrated from Germany to the United States in 1885. In the winter of 1909 his young son came to Canada and bought land, and in 1910 took up residence. He was only four years old when he accompanied his father from Germany and he lived in Chicago up to the time of migrating to this country. In 1914 he applied for naturalization and was rejected. He applied again in the spring of 1919, appeared before Judge Simmons, who accepted the application and forwarded it to Ottawa, but the Secretary of State at that time did not find it within his
discretion to grant naturalization. This applicant-I can speak for him personally-is a splendid type of citizen. He is anxious to become naturalized, but cannot undergo the expense of a third application. I have two or three cases of this kind. If a man wishes to become a Canadian citizen, but cannot afford the expense, is there any provision made in this bill to permit of his naturalization without further application?

There is no provision in the
bill now before the committee. If I followed my hon. friend correctly, this man was refused naturalization because the act then required ten years' residence?
Yes.

I am repealing that section
of the act and making the qualification five years. Whether or not the former application would be available at the present time I cannot say without giving the matter consideration. It might be possible for the judge before whom the man went to now certify to the applicant's qualifications, but I will look into, the matter. Maybe under the regulations we can do something.

I would
strongly recommend the minister to consider that suggestion very favourably because a wholly unnecessary hardship is being worked on these men who reside a long distance from the judges.

As I understand the situation, examinations were held very frequently during the first few years of the operations of the Civil Service Commission. Now, pretty lengthy lists of eligible candidates are on file and there is not the same necessity for holding examinations that there was formerly. That is the information I have received.

I wonder if the minister could tell us what procedure is followed in regard to these examinations. I have been given to understand that a man is sometimes appointed as a temporary employee and that he will remain in the office for six months during which time he becomes thoroughly familiar with the details of the work. At the end of the six months an examination will be called for and other men who, perhaps, have had just as much experience in clerical work as this particular man, are not in a position to compete with him because there are technical details connected with 'he work of the office with which he is more familiar, and this gives him an unfair advantage. The assumption, of course, is that if the commission want to retain a man in such a position all they have to do is to appoint him temporarily and then it will be comparatively easy for him to pass the examination over the heads of other men who are just as competent as he is in other respects. I wonder if the minister could tell us what the exact procedure is in such cases?

I am afraid it will not be possible for me to describe in any detailed way the operation- of the commission. If my hon. friend reouires information of that character I will secure the attendance of the secretary who is engaged before a committee upstairs. In the case of a temporary position, a temporary appointment is made. If the experience this employee has gained while holding the position temporarily gives him an advantage I suppose he would be entitled to it with this one exception: I have no doubt
